data.title: A different kind of ticket-splitting
data.description:
Going into Election Day, we heard a lot about potential ticket splitting in Texas. Maybe Republican Gov. Greg Abbott would win reelection while voters rejected Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Senate race.

That didn’t happen. Both men lost.

But a different kind of ticket splitting may have emerged elsewhere, and it’s worth paying attention to.

Democrats had a wildly good night on Tuesday. Republicans got obliterated. But further down the ballot, voters in some states that flipped to blue approved ballot questions that don’t exactly line up with the Democratic Party platform.

In Washington state, where Republicans haven’t won a governor’s race since 1980, nearly 57 percent of voters supported an initiative to keep males out of girls’ K-12 sports.

In Colorado, voters favored two measures: one requiring sex-based eligibility for school and college athletics and another prohibiting certain gender-related surgeries for minors.

Arizona voters supported restrictions involving school sports, bathrooms, and locker rooms.

In North Carolina, voters approved measures limiting taxation authority and expanding voter ID requirements. Florida voters approved a property tax reduction, while voters in Nevada and Ohio backed voter ID requirements.

We usually think of ticket splitting as voting for a Democrat in one race and a Republican in another. But what about voting for all Democrats while supporting ballot questions that reflect a position more commonly associated with Republicans?

We don’t know how many individual voters did exactly that, but the results suggest something that tends to get lost in all the red-versus-blue election coverage.

Someone can be furious about gas prices, fed up with corruption, frustrated with the direction of the country, or simply repelled by the candidates and still want policies they believe are fair and sensible when it comes to children and schools.

And voting against a Republican doesn’t mean rejecting every position associated with conservatives, any more than voting for a Democrat means embracing every position associated with progressives.

And then there’s the quality of the candidates themselves. Some were deeply flawed, some ran lousy (and lazy!) campaigns, and some seemed to think dissatisfaction with the other party was a substitute for giving voters an actual reason to support them.

That’s what makes the ballot questions so interesting. In some places, voters were rejecting the candidates but supporting their policy positions. 

Ballot questions offer something candidate races rarely do: the chance to weigh in on an issue without having to accept everything else that comes with a politician. A vote for governor or senator is a package deal. You’re choosing someone based on a whole collection of issues, priorities, promises, and personal qualities. You might agree with a candidate on five things and still decide the sixth is a dealbreaker. A ballot question strips all of that baggage. It asks voters to make a decision about one policy, without requiring them to sign on to everything else associated with a candidate they can’t stomach.

These ballot question fights are not over. In Washington state and Colorado, opponents are already discussing legal challenges to the measures that voters supported. What happens when the people elected to govern a state disagree with the voters on a specific issue?

And similar ballot questions could be coming to a state near you. A group of citizens recently dropped off signatures in hopes of setting up a women’s sports referendum in Maine, a state where we just saw a six-term Republican incumbent lose her Senate seat.

The blue wave turned out to be a tsunami and that makes these ballot question results even more interesting. If we really want to understand the electorate in these midterms, we need to pay attention to both.

Winning an election and winning an argument are definitely not the same thing.

Erika Sanzi is the senior director of communications for Defending Education.

data.title: Musk: 'Critical deals will be lost' at Nvidia without Huang
data.description:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on Saturday that Nvidia will lose “critical deals” after CEO Jensen Huang’s exit from the company following reports of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote in a post on social platform X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Huang’s resignation was announced Thursday following scrutiny over accusations stemming from a New York Times report in October that claimed American authorities discovered Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the now-former Nvidia chief.

The resignation came a day after the Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a separate affair with a Nvidia executive who reported to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

Musk has previously hinted his support for the former Nvidia CEO, saying it “would be an honor” to hire him, prior to his resignation, in response to a post on X.

President Trump, in a Truth Social post, suggested that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should be the one to take Jensen Huang’s place, saying, “there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple.”

“A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote in his post.

Following the initial Times report, Nvidia’s board had announced Sunday that it would initiate an independent investigation into the matter. On Tuesday, the company said it hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to conduct the investigation.

Huang admitted in a statement that he has been unfaithful to his wife, adding, “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” according to a report from Bloomberg. 

He was called by GOP lawmakers to appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s security protocols and his interactions with the alleged spy.

data.title: FAA ground stop leads to multiple delays, postponements in college football
data.description:
Friday’s nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has led to some changes in Saturday’s schedule for several college football games across the country.

The nationwide grounding began at around 4 p.m. EST and lasted several hours impacting travel plans for multiple teams including Ole Miss, Kansas State University, University of Utah and Arizona State University and University of Minnesota among others.

In the NCAA’s Big 12 Conference, games including Arizona State-UCF and Kansas-West Virginia were delayed by two hours from 3:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. EST on Saturday, USA Today reported. The Utah-Arizona kickoff was pushed to 10:30 p.m. EST, with the Utah team flying to Tucson Saturday morning.

In the Big Ten, Michigan State vs Washington has been moved back slightly to 5:30 p.m. It was originally scheduled for 4:15 p.m., the report said.

The Southeastern Conference’s Auburn-Mississippi State matchup was pushed back four hours from noon to 4:15 p.m., while Ole Miss-Oklahoma has been moved to Sunday at 1 p.m. EST, the conference updated in separate posts on social platform X.

The Ole Miss team was not able to depart on Friday due to the nationwide ground stop, and a late-night flight could not be accommodated, according to the statement. The team’s departure has been delayed until Saturday afternoon. The game was originally scheduled for 4:15 p.m. Saturday.

The FAA lifted the stop at around 8:15 p.m., Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed during a White House press briefing Friday night. He noted that the return to normal flight operations is expected to be “slow.”

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” Duffy said.

Duffy attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin adding the “public was never in danger in this process.”

data.title: Democrats win an election and immediately move to subvert democracy
data.description:
It appears democracy is too important to be left to voters.

After Democrats ran on “saving democracy” from its imminent destruction, many voters may be a bit confused by the actions of their newly elected representatives. Democratic politicians and pundits are moving to negate certain results in the last election and to circumvent future votes on key reforms. The country could soon be experiencing the greatest changes to our constitutional system in 250 years, but the public will have little to say about it.

In Seattle, socialist Mayor Katie Wilson announced that she and the city would move to block a statewide initiative approved by 36 of 39 counties. The public voted to require the separation of boys and girls in K-12 sports. It is an issue that has overwhelming support among both Democrats and Republicans, with polls showing roughly 70 percent of Americans supporting girls’ sports for girls alone.

But Wilson and others do not like the decision, so they are seeking to protect the public from their supposedly bad choices.

In Colorado, Governor-elect Phil Weiser (D), the former dean at the University of Colorado Law School, was a prominent figure in the “No Kings” protests before the election. But after his election, he decided that the voters’ democratic decisions on transgender policies were inherently flawed and he would have to correct them.

Colorado voters passed a ban on male athletes in girls and women’s sports. Proposition 134 defined girls as having female reproductive organs and boys as having male reproductive organs. So that there would be no ambiguity later, the drafters expressly added that “students assigned male at birth play only on boys teams or co-ed teams and vice versa for females.”

The public also passed Proposition 135, banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors.

Weiser, however, declared that, with a new supermajority in both houses, Democrats would “have to take a look at these anti-trans measures … to fix [them] and provide a much more human and sound approach.”

This is the same politician who recently insisted that he was “defending democracy” and standing for “our government of the people, by the people, and for the people.” But apparently, the last thing large-D Democrats want to do is actually listen to the people.

The “saving democracy” crowd seems to have a very serious problem with democracy.

In Alaska, the champions of democracy who supported Alaska Democratic Senatorial nominee Mary Peltola (D) worked to put a decoy “Dan Sullivan” on the ballot with the sole aim of confusing voters. The New York Times reported in painful detain that the effort had been coordinated at the highest level of the Democratic establishment, including the involvement of the law group of Marc Elias, the notorious lawyer involved in the Steele Dossier controversy.

In the prior election, many of these same figures supported efforts to prevent voters from voting for Trump and other Republicans — requiring the Supreme Court to step in and restore to the ballot the candidate who went on to win the popular vote.

Democrats are now planning to fundamentally change the constitutional system. As one Harvard law professor explained it, these committed democracy-defenders will guarantee that Republicans “never win another election.” The key is to prevent voters from actually voting on any of the changes.

Democratic leaders are openly talking about packing the Supreme Court to allow an array of changes by judicial fiat. Although many Americans still oppose court packing, this could technically be done by a vote of Congress.

There is also a building effort to effectively abolish the Electoral College, to increase the power of high-population blue states without actually seeking a constitutional amendment. Securing the White House after negating the Electoral College would mean that many of these changes could be accomplished by a simple majority vote.

There is also an effort to simply declare the District of Columbia a state, without a constitutional amendment to alter the status of D.C. as a federal enclave and non-state in Article I, Section 8. (Democrats are also seeking to add Puerto Rico, to give Democrats an even greater edge in the Senate.) Past polls show considerable opposition to making a state out of the federal district whose current boundaries were carved out of Maryland’s territory.

The key is to make these changes through Washington rather than giving citizens a vote on such fundamental changes. A packed court alone would bring radical changes, particularly with Democrats pointing to far-left Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson as their model for the new stacked court.

This has long been a pattern for far-left political movements. In my book “Rage and the Republic,” I discuss how the French radicals called the Jacobins took power by marshaling the rage of the people, but then ruled the nation as a small elite. While espousing faith in the “general will” of the people, the Jacobins concentrated power in the hands of brutal committees with such blood-soaked figures as  Maximilien Robespierre.

The Jacobins used the language of popular government to assume power, but not to share it with the people. While we have a representative democracy, the Framers still wanted citizens to approve major changes to our system. Today the new Jacobins are seeking structural changes to guarantee their own power while offering the voters ways to vent their rage rather than play a role in governance.

Taking another page from the Jacobins, Democratic leaders are promising heads. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) promised “many, many, many investigations” into what she calls the “criminals” of the opposing party. She even recently suggested that conservative Supreme Court justices might be impeached for ruling against the wishes of her party.

“I mean, of course, this Supreme Court as well has also kind of legalized a lot of his criminality,” she said. Of course, the standard for impeachment is not “kind of legalizing a lot.” But that is just the standard in the Constitution, which is itself becoming increasingly irrelevant to the Democratic Party’s agenda.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

data.title: 3,000+ flights canceled after FAA's ground stop
data.description:
U.S. air traffic is slowly returning to normal after a nationwide ground stop Friday halted flights and left thousands canceled and delayed.

As of Saturday morning, nearly 2,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. are delayed, and nearly 3,800 have been canceled, according to flight tracking website FlightAware.

FlightAware shows Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the busiest in the world, with the most delays — 54 — and the most cancellations — 85, followed by Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport.

Flights were grounded for hours on Friday, a rare move that has been used in only extraordinary circumstances — a human-error outage in 2023, and on Sept. 11, 2001, after the terror attacks. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) cited a telecommunications outage as the cause for the ground stop.

Even once the ground stop was lifted, delays and cancellations began to pile up and create a backlog that may take days to get back on track. Airlines began responding to the disruptions, offering waivers and special assistance to affected passengers.

United, Delta and Southwest all said they would waive all fare differences and change fees to allow passengers to change flights.

“Thank you for your patience as we work to restore our full schedule,” United Airlines wrote on the social platform X. “There are no fees to change your flight, and we’ll waive any fare difference.”

American Airlines waived change fees and is offering refunds, but still requires passengers to pay a fare difference.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that operations are “slowly returning to normal” Saturday morning, but that delays and cancellations will persist as adjustments are made to get air travel back on track.

“You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most,” Duffy wrote on X.

data.title: Greene calls Duffy, Mullin press briefing 'a shakedown for more money'
data.description:
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) accused Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin of using Friday’s nationwide ground stop to demand more taxpayer money, calling their joint press conference “unreal bulls—.”

“It doesn’t matter to any of them that the US Congress and every administration has spent like $15 trillion on foreign wars over the past 25 years but yeah you guys gotta fork over 50 billion more dollars so they can finally fix something in America,” Greene wrote in a post to the social platform X.

Representatives for the Department of Transportation and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights Friday afternoon, a rare move used previously in 2023, and before that, as a response to the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

The FAA cited a “temporary telecommunications outage,” which Duffy said was caused by a system “overloaded with data” that forced them to shut it down.

In the press conference, Duffy said he wanted $50 billion in funding for modernizing the air traffic control system — a key priority of his as transportation secretary.

“I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

While Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack or anything nefarious, he said they would not rule anything out. Greene claimed they were lying and that it was “obviously” a cyberattack, without evidence.

The FAA recently rolled out an AI-powered air traffic control tool, called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) program. The tool debuted first in the Washington, D.C. area and cost the department $875 million.

Air Space Intelligence, the company behind SMART, issued a statement Friday night denying any link to the ground stop, which Duffy echoed during the briefing.

The transportation secretary shared his message to members of Congress requesting increased funding.

“Give President Trump — give Duffy the money. Let them finish this job so we don’t have to do a press conference at 8:30 at night ever again,” Duffy said.

data.title: The new center of gravity in Europe
data.description:
Last week, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that Poland had thwarted a Russian provocation along its border with Moscow’s Kaliningrad exclave. The episode underscores a larger reality: The frontline of European security runs through Central Europe, and the continent’s center of gravity has shifted. 

Central and Northern European states are becoming Europe’s economic backbone and increasingly its military one. They occupy a strategic space that is both a focal point of Russian pressure and a target of Chinese influence. 

As Western Europe’s traditional centers of political and economic power contend with domestic pressures and political instability, Central and Northern European nations are assuming a greater role in the continent’s growth, industrial renewal and defense. 

The region is home to some of the European Union’s fastest-growing economies. In 2025, Poland’s GDP grew by 3.6 percent, Lithuania’s by 2.9 percent and the Czech Republic’s by 2.6 percent. 

Germany’s industrial engine, weakened by high energy costs and Chinese competition, remains Europe’s largest and most important economy and manufacturing base. But its established industrial hubs are increasingly complemented by capacity across the Czech Republic, Estonia, Lithuania, Poland and Slovakia. These countries have recently outperformedin new industrial enterprise births per capita. Europe’s industrial strength is expanding eastward. 

The region is also an emerging innovation hub. Affordable operating costs, highly skilled talent and strong research institutions have fueled entrepreneurial ecosystems in Prague, Riga, Tallinn and Warsaw. 

Better integration of these industrial and technological strengths could create more secure European supply chains — and significant opportunities for the United States. A thriving integrated tech-industrial corridor in Central Europe will attract American investment, create partnerships for U.S. firms and strengthen the transatlantic economic motor.  

Realizing this potential will require secure, affordable energy. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Europe has learned the costs of dependence on Russian hydrocarbons. Diversifying energy supplies and expanding interconnectors, pipelines and storage capacity will give Europe the means to eventually eliminate its remaining dependence on Russian energy. 

But Europe must avoid replacing one strategic vulnerability with another. China’s dominance of green technology supply chains presents a significant challenge. The United States can help address it. Beyond liquified natural gas exports, American companies can partner with European counterparts on civil nuclear technology, including small modular reactors, electricity grid modernization and efforts to diversify green technology supply chains away from China. 

Militarily, Central Europe is becoming an essential pillar of NATO. Poland fields the alliance’s third-largest military, behind only the United States and Turkey. The region also leads in defense investment. Lithuania, Estonia and Poland, which invest 5.33 percent, 5.10 percentand 4.68 percent of GDP, respectively, are approaching or already exceeding the alliance’s ambitious defense spending benchmark adopted at NATO’s Hague Summit. 

Germany’s transformation is equally consequential. On track to spend $147 billion on defense in 2026, Germany’s defense budget this year will exceed the combined 2022 defense budgets of France, Germany and Italy. 

Berlin has set an ambitious goal of developing the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional military. In April, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius outlined plans to expand Germany’s military to 460,000 by 2039. If realized, German and Polish military expansion would create a formidable conventional defense core at the heart of NATO. 

But military strength depends on more than spending and troop numbers. As Palantir Chief Technical Officer Shyam Sankar observed at a public forum last month: “Your deterrence was never your stockpile… It was your ability to generate the stockpile.” Central Europe’s industrial capacity and ability to scale production will be critical to deterring and, if necessary, defending against Russian aggression. 

Beyond the renewal of military capabilities, Central and Northern European infrastructure is also critical to collective defense. The region provides strategic depth and is home to key depots, logistical corridors and staging areas that could prove decisive in a future conflict with Russia. The geography of Europe dictates that infrastructure in places like the Czech Republic, Germany and Poland will factor significantly into any future war. 

No discussion of Europe’s security architecture is complete without Ukraine. Its sovereignty, territorial integrity and successful integration into European economic and security structures are essential to a secure transatlantic future. Ukraine’s defeat, by contrast, would profoundly undermine it.  

The arteries already connecting Ukraine to the region have enormous potential to mature and expand. Growing ties to Ukraine, particularly its defense industrial capacity, can further energize the core of European economic and military power. 

Faced with acute challenges posed by an authoritarian axis and increasingly constrained resources, the United States must recognize that its future security depends in large part on factoring the strength and production capacities of its allies into its strategic calculations. 

Nowhere is this more important than in Central Europe. Its geography, population, technological innovation, industrial base and expanding military capabilities make it an indispensable pillar of American engagement in Europe. 

Our adversaries recognize the region’s importance as well. The region is a prime target of persistent Russian grey-zone attacks and information warfare, while Beijing has worked assiduously to weaken its ties with the United States. 

The heart of Europe is emerging as a chief architect of the continent’s future; Washington should treat it accordingly. 

Daniel Kochis is a senior fellow in the Center on Europe and Eurasia at Hudson Institute.

data.title: Live updates: US air travel recovers from ground stop; Federalist Society gathers following blue wave
data.description:
U.S. airports and airlines are still playing catch up on Saturday following Friday’s four hour long nationwide ground, with travelers across the country scrambling to get to their destinations after facing delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday night he expects the transition back to normal air travel to be “slow” following the rare grounding, which he attributed to a data overload and outdated air traffic control systems.

While members of his cabinet took the podium to discuss the Federal Aviation Administration’s move, President Trump stayed silent on the stoppage throughout Friday afternoon. He has no public events scheduled over the weekend.

Meanwhile, the Federalist Society — a conservative legal organization — is convening in Washington for the second day of its annual “National Lawyers Convention.” During its opening night, Secretary of State Marco Rubio took the stage, adopting an optimistic tone of American idealism amid buzz surrounding his alleged interest in launching a presidential campaign. The Hill’s Laura Kelly has more.

Meanwhile, several midterm races have yet to be called over a week out from Election Day — including the contentious Alaska Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and Democrat Mary Peltola.

Follow live below

data.title: Peltola holds nearly 4-point lead on Sullivan in latest ballot drop
data.description:
Democrat Mary Peltola has again expanded her lead in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race with more votes counted, now ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) by nearly 4 points, or more than 10,000 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Peltola netted nearly 2,000 votes from the latest batch of votes added.

The Alaska Democrat now has 49.8 percent of the vote, just shy of a majority, which she would need to avoid an instant runoff using ranked choice voting. With 91 percent of votes counted, the former congresswoman now has a real chance to surpass 50 percent.

In a statement shared to the social platform X on Friday, Peltola’s campaign again declared victory after the new vote drop.

“There is no mathematical path for Sullivan to win this race,” the statement reads. “When the remaining votes are counted, Mary will decisively be elected as Alaska’s next United States Senator.”

Sullivan’s campaign account has not posted since Nov. 4. DDHQ has not called this race as of Saturday morning.

Votes from Alaska will continue to trickle in throughout next week, but all must be counted and reported by Nov. 18. If Peltola still does not reach a majority of the vote by then, the ranked choice voting tabulation would take place.

Peltola avoiding ranked choice is potentially significant in another way. The Trump administration previously sued to block the certification of the Senate race if Sullivan lost, because of the presence of another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot.

The Justice Department argued that if Peltola won by less than the amount of votes the non-incumbent Sullivan received, then they could argue the candidate’s presence confused voters. That lawsuit was ultimately dismissed, and if Peltola’s current lead holds, the administration would not be able to make the same case.

A win for Peltola would be significant for Democrats, giving the party a 56th Senate seat after its already strong midterm performance. It would also make it less likely that the GOP would be able to win back the chamber in 2028, even if they win the presidency.

Elsewhere in Alaska, DDHQ projected that Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the gubernatorial contest, a pickup for Democrats. The U.S. House race is still uncalled, but Rep. Nick Begich III (R) leads. DDHQ projected that contest would go to ranked choice voting.

data.title: Murderers face justice decades later. Why are child-rapists protected from older charges?
data.description:
Legally, there is a strange disconnect between how this country treats the crime of murder and how it treats the crime of sexually abusing a child. In too many jurisdictions, accused child-abusers are granted legal protections and advantages that people who have been accused of murder do not have access to. 

Yet, in numerous surveys, most adults rank the crime of rape as roughly equivalent to that of murder.

The crime of raping a child stands at the very summit of most people’s ideas of criminality at its most horrific. Legal minds and policymakers from across the political spectrum agree on this. In the wake of the controversial Supreme Court decision in 2008’s Kennedy vs. Louisiana, presidential candidate Barack Obama found himself agreeing with Justice Samuel Alito’s dissent, in which he wrote, “In the eyes of ordinary Americans, the very worst child-rapists … are the epitome of moral depravity.” 

Yet in many parts of the U.S., those who rape children are protected by statutes of limitations. Unlike murderers, they cannot be made to stand trial for their crimes after a certain number of years has passed. In more than half of the U.S., that limit is pegged to the age of the victim. In other words, once victims pass that age, ranging anywhere from 24 to 55, they lose the right to bring charges against their attackers. In many cases, they even expose themselves to slander charges by going public with their claims after the lapse of many years. 

This is a big problem for victims.

If someone is murdered, a corpse is usually enough to trigger a criminal investigation. But when children are sexually abused, they need to file convincing reports with the proper authorities for anything to happen. Studies have shown that more than half of the victims of child sexual abuse wait until they are past the age of 50 before they come forward. It is common for abusers to swear the children to secrecy and threaten them with further consequences in the event of disclosure. The shame and trauma of the attack are usually enough on their own to ensure silence for years to come.

In my own case, after being raped by my violin professor at the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia when I was 14, I made all of the usual mistakes. For months, I closed up, kept to myself and did nothing. Then I asked the dean to give me a new teacher. He scoffed at the idea and dragged his feet on taking action. After another painful year, I attempted suicide and then left Curtis. Decades passed before I went public with my story, in a cover feature in The Philadelphia Inquirer in 2019. 

Unfortunately, even though Pennsylvania passed a new law that year setting the higher cutoff age of 55 for childhood victims of sexual abuse to file charges, this applied only to new cases. It did nothing for people like me or other past victims of abuse. Under the applicable laws at the time, I had two years from the time of the attack in 1986 to file charges. The deadline expired when I was 16, emotionally and financially broken. It’s ridiculous to imagine that I could have lawyered up and done anything concrete to stop my attacker at that time.

Child rapists know this. They go after the most vulnerable kids, and they understand exactly how to game the laws that are intended to deter them. The institutions that shelter these people have also shown a keen awareness of just how much, or how little, is required of them to fulfill their obligations under the law. 

And that is why federal legislation is needed to close the loopholes and harmonize the hodgepodge of laws against sexual abuse of children abuse that currently exist in the U.S.

There is no divergence of public opinion on whether the sexual abuse of children is good or bad. There is a rock-solid consensus across the political spectrum that it should be stamped out as much as possible. Childhood sex abuse ruins lives. It is more pernicious than simple murder. There are certain circumstances in which killing someone is fully defensible, ethically and under the law, but no one ever raped a child in self-defense. 

The only force standing in the way of justice for victims is a narrow set of vested institutional interests seeking to limit their financial exposure to potential claims. That is not a good enough reason to protect child-rapists. American voters do not want their elected representatives to protect criminals. Congress needs to take action and strip them of their protections once and for all.

Lara St. John is a violinist and filmmaker. Her documentary, “Dear Lara,” on sexual abuse at music schools will be screened at the Alexandria Film Festival on Nov. 15.
